analysis|05-16|1568|Η Μαίρη Στιούαρτ φτάνει στην Αγγλία|Mary, Queen of Scots Arrives in England|Mary Stuart had come to the Scottish throne as an infant, and her reign was turbulent, with political rivalries and religious divisions. In 1567 she was forced to abdicate in favour of her son, and afterwards she lost her power following a defeat. Her life was bound up with the rivalry between Catholicism and Protestantism in the British Isles. Elizabeth was a Protestant queen, and Mary's presence, as a Catholic, was regarded as a source of danger to the stability of the realm. // In May 1568 the queen took refuge in England, hoping that Elizabeth I would protect her. Instead of a welcome, she found herself under arrest, since Elizabeth feared plots around her person. Her confinement lasted about nineteen years in various castles, and Mary kept part of her court. Her detention was restricted to a succession of castles in England. // Mary's stay in England became the occasion for conspiracies and diplomatic disputes, and it ultimately led to her trial and execution in 1587. Her son James later became king of both Scotland and England, thus uniting the two thrones. This episode remains one of the best-known chapters of British history. The story of the executed queen has become a source for literature, theatre and film.

analysis|05-16|1916|Η συμφωνία Σάικς-Πικό|The Sykes-Picot Agreement|During the First World War the Ottoman Empire fought on the side of the Central Powers, and the Allies discussed what would happen to the Arab regions of the empire after victory. Britain had given promises of Arab independence, while France and Russia claimed influence in the region. These contradictory promises created intense tension. The need for alliances in the war led the powers to make promises of territory that they could not guarantee at the same time. // On 16 May 1916 the diplomats Mark Sykes of Britain and François Georges-Picot of France signed a secret agreement. By it, territories of the Middle East were divided into zones of influence, with Britain and France controlling areas that could be administered directly or indirectly. The agreement remained secret, without the knowledge of the Arab peoples. The negotiations took place without the participation of the Arab peoples, and the text provided for zones of direct or indirect influence. // The agreement contradicted the promises made to the Arabs and influenced the drawing of borders after the war. When it became known, after the Russian Revolution, it provoked anger and suspicion in the region. Modern disputes over borders and sovereignty in the Middle East often refer back to this agreement as their starting point. The agreement is one of the most frequently cited examples of the international consequences of secret diplomatic arrangements.

analysis|05-16|1920|Η Ιωάννα της Λωραίνης αγία|Joan of Arc Is Canonised|Joan of Lorraine, known as Jeanne d'Arc, was a peasant woman who, according to her own testimony, heard voices calling her to help France. During the Hundred Years' War with England, France was in a difficult position and many of its regions were under foreign control. Joan led military operations that strengthened the morale of the French. Her era was charged with religious feeling, and the appearance of a young woman with a mission made a strong impression. // Her actions linked her with King Charles VII, but in 1430 she was captured by the Burgundians and handed over to the English. Her trial was held under strong political pressure and ended with her execution in 1431. Her course left deep marks on the memory of the country. Her trial continued even after her death, with a review that annulled the convictions in 1456. // The canonisation of 1920 made official her position as a national heroine of France and linked religious and national identity. Her figure appears in works of art, literature and public ceremonies, and her story is still discussed for its relation to the Church and to politics. The pope's decision was also an act of rehabilitation for a woman who had been condemned in her own time. Her modern figure is especially popular in France, where her feast is celebrated every May.

analysis|05-16|1929|Απονέμονται τα πρώτα Όσκαρ|The First Academy Awards Are Presented|In the late 1920s cinema was changing after the introduction of sound. The American film industry sought to gain prestige and to promote cooperation between artists and studios. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences was founded in 1927 with the aim of honouring the achievements of the field. The Academy was initially intended to limit disputes between the studios and the artists of the industry. // The first presentation of the awards took place on 16 May 1929 at an event in Los Angeles. The ceremony was very short, and the awards concerned works of the previous period. The attendance of the public was limited compared with today's great evenings. The audience of the period was limited, and the event took place without live television broadcast. // The 1929 presentation laid the foundations for an institution that is today among the best known in the world. The rules and the process changed over the years, and the ceremony became a global event with international television broadcast. The importance of the first evening lies in the fact that it set the relationship between the industry and public recognition of artists. The Oscars institution today has enormous influence on the industry, and its presentation attracts millions of viewers around the world.

analysis|05-16|1960|Ο Θίοντορ Μάιμαν παρουσιάζει το πρώτο λέιζερ|Theodore Maiman Presents the First Laser|In the mid-twentieth century physics had developed the theory of light emission from excited atoms, and the idea of stimulated emission had been proposed decades earlier. The scientific community sought ways to produce coherent light. Theodore Maiman, an American physicist, worked on this problem. Research on lasers was linked with the rivalry between research laboratories in the Cold War era. // On 16 May 1960 Maiman presented the operation of the first laser device, which used a ruby crystal as the active medium. Using a powerful lamp of light he aimed at the crystal, and it emitted a coherent beam of red light. The news was published shortly afterwards and drew the attention of the scientific community. Maiman used a powerful lamp and mirrors at the ends of the crystal, so that the emission of light was amplified. // The laser became one of the most important tools of modern technology. It is used in medicine for surgical operations, in telecommunications through optical fibres, and in the measurement and processing of materials. The invention opened an entire branch of optics, and its history shows how a theoretical idea can become a means of everyday life. Today lasers are a basic part of modern digital infrastructure.

analysis|05-17|1940|Οι Γερμανοί μπαίνουν στις Βρυξέλλες|The Germans Enter Brussels|In May 1940 Germany had launched an attack on the Low Countries and France, bypassing the Maginot Line. Belgium had declared neutrality, but it found itself immediately in the field of battle. King Leopold III tried to keep the army in battle, but the advance was rapid. Germany had applied a strategy of rapid movements with armoured units, which surprised its opponents. // The German army crossed Belgian territory and on 17 May 1940 entered Brussels, the capital of the country. The government had already left the city, and the occupation took place without great resistance in the centre. The entry of the troops strengthened the sense that European defence had collapsed. Belgian soldiers resisted at some points, but the army could not withstand the pressure for long. // The occupation of Brussels was one of the first steps of an occupation that would last until 1944, and the military surrender of Belgium in May 1940 left a contested memory. The occupation affected the economy, daily life and the administration of the country. The city became a centre of German administration, and this day remains as the start of a difficult period. Brussels returned to Allied control in 1944, and the memory of the occupation remains alive in the country.

analysis|05-17|1954|Απόφαση «Μπράουν κατά Συμβουλίου Παιδείας»|Brown v. Board of Education Decision|After the American Civil War the Southern states had passed laws imposing racial segregation, known as the Jim Crow laws. In 1896 the Supreme Court had justified segregation with the principle of "separate but equal". In practice the facilities for black people were inferior, and the education of black children was especially unequal. American public education was then divided into white and black schools, with clear differences in resources. // The Brown v. Board of Education case concerned a family in Topeka, Kansas, who challenged racial discrimination in schools. On 17 May 1954 the court, by a unanimous decision, ruled that segregation in public schools violated constitutional equality. The opinion of the court was delivered by its chief justice, Earl Warren. The decision was accompanied by calls for gradual implementation, and many areas of the South met it with strong resistance. // The decision challenged the system of segregation as a whole and gave impetus to the civil rights movement. Its implementation, however, was slow and often met with resistance, until new laws followed in the 1960s. The case remains one of the most important judicial texts in American history. The case opened the way for the subsequent legal battles of the civil rights movement.

analysis|05-18|1565|Αρχίζει η πολιορκία της Μάλτας|The Siege of Malta Begins|Malta was the seat of the Order of the Knights of St John, which had settled on the island in 1530 after losing Rhodes. The Knights formed a naval and military force against the Ottoman Empire and controlled navigation in the Mediterranean. Suleiman the Magnificent regarded the island as an important point for control of the area. The island had strategic importance because of its position between Italy and North Africa. // In May 1565 the Ottoman fleet and army landed on the island and began the siege. The Knights, together with the locals, defended the forts of Malta, and the attacks of the Ottomans proved fruitless for a long time. Their resistance caused heavy losses to the attacking forces. The siege included hard battles around Fort St Elmo, where the defence was particularly fierce. // The siege ended with the withdrawal of the Ottomans in the autumn, when reinforcements arrived from Spain and Sicily. The successful defence strengthened the prestige of the Order and of Malta in Europe, and the role of the island as a fortress of the Mediterranean continued. The event is regarded as one of the great military episodes of the period. The resistance of Malta became a symbol of the endurance of small states against larger forces.

analysis|05-18|1804|Ο Ναπολέων αυτοκράτορας|Napoleon Becomes Emperor|After the Revolution of 1789 France changed its form of government several times, and the Directory was unstable. Napoleon Bonaparte had gained great popularity through his military victories and carried out a coup in 1799. As First Consul he practically governed France, while his power was strengthened by new laws. The rise of Napoleon reflected society's desire for stability after years of internal conflict. // On 18 May 1804 the French Senate proclaimed him Emperor of the French. The decision was ratified by a referendum, and the coronation took place in Paris in December of the same year, where he himself placed the crown on his head. The move symbolised the transition from a republic to a new, imperial form of power. Napoleon took the title with the consent of the institutions, and the process combined legitimation with his own will for strong power. // The empire of Napoleon brought reforms, such as the Civil Code, which influenced many countries. At the same time the wars that followed changed the map of Europe for years. The beginning of the empire marked the end of the original revolutionary ideas of the republic in France. The empire lasted until 1814, and the notion of a strong executive influenced the later political systems of Europe.

analysis|05-18|1980|Εκρήγνυται το ηφαίστειο Σεντ Χέλενς|Mount St. Helens Erupts|Mount St. Helens in the state of Washington is a volcano of the Cascade Range, and it had shown signs of awakening in the preceding months. Earthquakes and gas emissions had increased the fear of an eruption. The authorities had evacuated a zone around the mountain, but many residents and scientists remained close to it. The volcanoes of the Cascade Range belong to a subduction zone, where the Pacific oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate. // On 18 May 1980 a huge eruption destroyed the northern part of the volcano, and an enormous cloud of ash was thrown to a great height. Landslides and lava flows destroyed forests and the surrounding areas, and many people were killed, among them scientists and locals. The disaster changed the landscape over a wide area. The eruption caused a lateral collapse of the mountain, which was rare and particularly dangerous. // The eruption is regarded as the deadliest volcanic eruption in the history of the United States and led to better volcano monitoring systems. The scientific community learned much about the behaviour of volcanoes and about the dangers of volcanic ash clouds for aviation. Mount St. Helens remains a living example of the relationship between nature and human life. The recording and analysis of the eruption helped improve the monitoring of other volcanoes in America.

analysis|05-19|1536|Αποκεφαλίζεται η Άννα Μπολέιν|Anne Boleyn Is Beheaded|Henry VIII of England wanted a divorce from Catherine of Aragon in order to marry Anne Boleyn. Rome did not allow the divorce, and the king broke away from the Catholic Church, establishing the Church of England with himself as its head. This change radically altered the relations of the state with Rome. The break with Rome allowed the king to control church property, which strengthened his financial position. // In May 1536 Anne was accused of adultery and other offences, in a trial that many regarded as a frame-up. She was executed at the Tower of London on 19 May 1536, while the king moved quickly to a new marriage. The execution was one of the most dramatic moments of his reign. Anne had attained the position of queen, while the accusations against her were linked with the political rivalry of the court. // Anne Boleyn remains in history as a wife who was executed, and as the mother of Queen Elizabeth I. The case has been discussed for centuries, and many historians consider that the charges had political motives. The religious reform begun with this affair shaped English history for decades. The marriage and execution of Anne have remained in memory as a basic element of English Renaissance history.

analysis|05-19|1919|Ο Κεμάλ αποβιβάζεται στη Σαμψούντα|Kemal Lands at Samsun|After the First World War the Ottoman Empire was dismembered, with the Allied forces controlling part of Constantinople and other areas. The Treaty of Sèvres, in 1920, provided for large territorial losses. A nationalist movement under Mustafa Kemal developed in Anatolia, opposing the terms of the Allies. The Ottoman government in Constantinople was in a state of weakness, and power was divided between local leaders and the military. // On 19 May 1919 Mustafa Kemal landed at Samsun on the Black Sea coast, with an official mission to inspect the region. From there he began to organise the national movement, with congresses and local resistance groups. For the Greeks of Pontus the day is remembered in connection with the events that followed, which is why they commemorate it as the Day of Remembrance of the Pontic Genocide. Kemal's appearance in the region strengthened the organisation of the movement, and the first congresses brought together representatives from various provinces. // The national movement led to the war of Anatolia and the founding of modern Turkey, with the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. For the Greek communities of Pontus the events of the period were tragic, with deportations and deaths that deeply affected an entire society. The 19th of May remains important in the memory of the Pontians and in the international debate on genocide. The day is a national holiday in Turkey, and the different interpretation of it by the two peoples continues to affect the relations between the two countries.

analysis|05-20|1498|Ο Βάσκο ντα Γκάμα φτάνει στην Ινδία|Vasco da Gama Reaches India|In the fifteenth century the Portuguese sought a sea route to India, in order to bypass the overland trade networks controlled by the Arabs and the Venetians. Portugal had developed navigation along the coasts of Africa. Henry the Navigator had encouraged expeditions along the African coast, with the aim of finding new trade routes. Vasco da Gama undertook the voyage that would reach India. // On 20 May 1498 da Gama arrived at Calicut, on the south coast of India, and became the first European to reach India by sea around Africa. The reception by the local rulers was cautious, and the negotiations for trade were difficult. The voyage was very costly in lives, as many sailors died of disease. Da Gama negotiated with the local ruler, but the Arab merchants of the region resisted the presence of the Portuguese. // The sea route opened a new era for trade, and Portuguese ships dominated it for several decades. The change affected the commercial balances of Europe, Asia and Africa. The voyage of da Gama is regarded as one of the most important naval achievements of the age of the great discoveries. This route gave Portugal a strong advantage in the spice trade for several decades.

analysis|05-20|1873|Πατεντάρονται τα τζιν του Λέβι Στράους|Levi Strauss's Jeans Are Patented|In the mid-nineteenth century California saw a large influx of people searching for gold. Levi Strauss, a textile merchant of German origin, sold durable fabrics to workers and miners. The tailor Jacob Davis, a customer of his, had the idea of reinforcing the pockets of trousers with metal rivets. The demand for durable and cheap work clothes had increased in California because of migration and mining. // On 20 May 1873 the invention was patented in the United States. The trousers with metal rivets in the pockets were intended for workers who needed durable clothing. The innovation was very successful, and this model was the first form of the modern jeans. The method of adding the rivets was simple but effective, and it reduced the frequency of wear on the pockets. // Jeans evolved from working clothes into an everyday garment worn by all social classes. The history of the Levi Strauss company is an example of how a practical solution can become a global fashion symbol. Jeans later became connected with new cultures and different fashion eras. The history of jeans shows how a small technical solution can affect the daily lives of millions of people.

analysis|05-20|1927|Ο Λίντμπεργκ ξεκινά τη διάσχιση του Ατλαντικού|Lindbergh begins his Atlantic crossing|Until 1927 no pilot had managed to cross the Atlantic alone in a direct flight. The first crossing of the Atlantic by air had been made in 1919, but with intermediate stops. The idea of a large cash prize for the flight from New York to Paris had attracted the attention of many pilots. The flight was prepared with careful planning, and the aircraft had a large fuel tank for the duration of the journey. // On 20 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh took off in his single-engined aircraft, the Spirit of St. Louis, for a non-stop flight. He was alone in the cockpit, and the flight lasted hours, with great danger from weather and fatigue. Lindbergh flew towards the European coast without stopping anywhere. Lindbergh had started as an airmail pilot and had gained experience over long distances. // The flight became world news and made him famous. It showed the potential of aviation for long-distance transport and gave impetus to the development of the aviation industry. The act is regarded as one of the best-known achievements of early aviation. The boldness of the flight contributed to a wave of enthusiasm for aviation, which influenced investment and research in the years that followed.

analysis|05-20|2002|Ανεξάρτητο το Ανατολικό Τιμόρ|East Timor Becomes Independent|East Timor was a Portuguese colony until the mid-1970s, and after Portugal's departure Indonesia annexed it militarily. The occupation was accompanied by serious human rights violations and by resistance from the locals. The international community did not recognise the annexation, and the issue remained open for decades. The Indonesian occupation was a cause of confrontation with the international community, since many countries did not recognise the annexation. // In 1999, after a referendum in which the inhabitants voted for independence, violence followed that led to United Nations intervention. The United Nations transitional administration took over the governance and prepared the country for full independence. On 20 May 2002 East Timor officially became an independent state. The referendum of 1999 was held under UN supervision, and the result was clearly in favour of independence despite pressures. // Independence was a historic victory for a people who had resisted for years. The new state faced difficult problems of development, infrastructure and political stability. The case of Timor is one of the best-known examples of self-determination in modern international history. The independence of East Timor strengthened the debate on the role of the UN in transitional administrations and on the limits of international intervention.

analysis|05-21|878|Πέφτει η Συρακούσα|Syracuse Falls|Syracuse was one of the most important cities of Byzantine Sicily, and the island was at the centre of a long conflict between Byzantium and the Arabs. The Arabs had begun conquering Sicily from 827, and the empire's territories on the island were shrinking. The city had a long history as an important port and cultural centre, with Greek roots and great radiance in the Mediterranean. The siege of the city was part of this long campaign. // Syracuse fell to the Arabs in 878, after a long siege. Its capture was a crushing blow to the Byzantine presence on the island, and the city had played a major role in the defence of the region. The siege lasted months, and the resistance of the inhabitants was remarkable, though it did not prevent the final capture. Its fall was recorded as an important event in the sources of the period. // With the fall of Syracuse Byzantine rule in Sicily was gradually limited, and the island changed its culture and religious life for centuries. The Arab period of Sicily left noticeable traces in language, architecture and the economy. The fall is regarded as an important point in the long history of the Mediterranean. The history of Syracuse remains the subject of archaeological research, which illuminates the life of the city in different periods.

analysis|05-21|1871|Αρχίζει η Ματωμένη Εβδομάδα|The Bloody Week Begins|After the defeat of France in the war of 1870 and the capture of Napoleon III, the country was in deep political crisis. In Paris the Commune was established, a revolutionary government that opposed the government of Thiers, which had its seat at Versailles. The Commune demanded autonomy for the city and implemented social reforms. The uprising of the Commune had broken out in an atmosphere of siege, since Paris had been surrounded in the preceding months. // On 21 May 1871 the government's troops entered Paris and repression began, which became known as the Bloody Week. The fighting took place street by street, with a heavy cost for the civilian population. The Commune collapsed within a few days, and crowds of people were arrested, executed or exiled. The inhabitants of the working-class quarters defended the barricades, and the fighting was particularly fierce in the centre of the city. // The Bloody Week left deep marks on French politics and society. The repression created memories of conflict that for years shaped the relationship of the state with the labour movements. The Paris Commune remains in history as a point of reference for every revolutionary movement. The event has been widely studied by historians, who discuss the number of victims and the responsibilities of all sides.

analysis|05-21|1881|Ιδρύεται ο Ερυθρός Σταυρός των ΗΠΑ|The American Red Cross Is Founded|In 1863 the International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva, on the initiative of Henry Dunant, with the aim of helping the wounded in wars. The idea gradually spread, and international conventions were established for the protection of the wounded and of civilians. In the United States, however, there was not yet a national organisation following this logic. The American war had left countless wounded and missing, and the need for organised help was pressing. // Clara Barton, a nurse who had served in the Civil War, laid the foundations for the American organisation. On 21 May 1881 the founding of the American Red Cross became official, and Barton became its first president. The organisation began with disaster relief and voluntary activities. Barton travelled to battlefields and to affected areas to distribute medical help, and became known for her tireless work. // The American Red Cross became one of the largest humanitarian organisations in the United States. Its activity extended to natural disasters, wars and blood donation services. Its history shows how the idea of humanitarian help passed from the battlefields into the everyday life of communities. Its contribution is regarded as one of the basic elements of American humanitarian tradition, and the organisation continues its work today.

analysis|05-21|1904|Ιδρύεται η FIFA|FIFA Is Founded|At the beginning of the twentieth century football had spread rapidly across many countries, but there was no single international body to coordinate matches. The national federations operated independently, and international matches were played under different rules. Europe had become the centre of football activity, and international matches between national teams were becoming ever more frequent. The need for coordination was increasingly evident in Europe. // On 21 May 1904 representatives of federations from several European countries met in Paris and founded the Fédération Internationale de Football Association, known as FIFA. The new organisation undertook to set common rules and to organise international matches. The founding took place at informal meetings, and its aim was the cooperation of the national federations. // FIFA became the central institution of world football and today organises the World Cup. In recent years its activity has been discussed in terms of transparency and governance, but its role in international football life remains decisive. The founding of 1904 was the first step towards a worldwide code for the sport. International competitions, such as the World Cup which began in 1930, gave FIFA a strong position in international sporting life.

analysis|05-21|1927|Ο Λίντμπεργκ προσγειώνεται στο Παρίσι|Lindbergh Lands in Paris|Lindbergh's flight from New York had begun the previous day. The pilot flew over the Atlantic without a companion, and the weather conditions were difficult. The flight was a great challenge, with danger to the pilot's life from the weather and from the lack of navigation instruments. Fatigue was a constant problem, and the pilot faced serious difficulties during the night. // On 21 May 1927 Lindbergh landed at Le Bourget airport near Paris, after a flight lasting about 33 hours. A large crowd of spectators had gathered, and the welcome was warm. The French welcomed the pilot with enthusiasm, and the news spread immediately through the press of Europe and America. Lindbergh instantly became a global hero. // The landing in Paris gave Lindbergh international fame and showed that the crossing of the Atlantic in a single aircraft was feasible. The success accelerated the development of aviation and strengthened public confidence in aeroplanes. The moment remains one of the best-known in the history of aviation. Lindbergh received many honours, and his feat gave impetus to the development of commercial aviation in the 1930s.

analysis|05-21|1998|Παραιτείται ο Σουχάρτο|Suharto Resigns|Suharto had governed Indonesia since 1967, after a transfer of power that included mass killings of communists. His rule was based on authoritarian measures, a strong army and economic development. This stability was accompanied by corruption, restrictions on freedoms and the absence of free elections. Indonesia had previously faced problems, such as regional tensions and difficulties in developing its island territory. // The Asian financial crisis of 1997 struck Indonesia deeply, with the collapse of the currency, unemployment and rising prices. Discontent spread, and mass demonstrations, with students in the forefront, demanded change. In May 1998 the situation became explosive. The demonstrators demanded reforms and the fight against corruption, and the police responded with violence in several cases. // Suharto's resignation brought an end to a long period of authoritarianism. A transitional period followed, with new elections and the strengthening of democratic institutions. The transition was not easy, but Indonesia later became one of the largest democracies in the world. The transition to a democratic system was a period of uncertainty but also an important moment in the modern history of Southeast Asia. The development affected public life and citizens' understanding of their rights.

analysis|05-22|1859|Γεννιέται ο Άρθουρ Κόναν Ντόιλ|Arthur Conan Doyle Is Born|Arthur Conan Doyle grew up in a Catholic family in Scotland, with a strong connection to literature. He studied medicine in Edinburgh and worked as a doctor before turning to writing. His experiences of medicine and the powers of observation of doctors influenced his literary work. Scotland in the nineteenth century had a strong tradition in education and science, which shaped the young writer. // Doyle was born in Edinburgh on 22 May 1859. His birth marks the beginning of the biography of one of the best-known authors of detective novels. From there begins the story that after decades would give the world Sherlock Holmes. Doyle combined his professional interests with literature, and his first stories were published in periodicals of the period. // Sherlock Holmes first appeared in 1887 and became one of the most recognisable characters in literature. His method, based on observation and analysis, influenced the detective novel and the culture of detectives. Doyle wrote other works too, but the popularity of Holmes remains undiminished. His contribution to the literature of crime remains recognised, and his works have been adapted in many forms, from theatre to cinema.

analysis|05-22|1960|Ο μεγαλύτερος σεισμός που έχει καταγραφεί|The Largest Earthquake Ever Recorded|Chile lies along the fault where the Nazca and South American tectonic plates converge. The region is one of the most seismically active in the world, and earthquakes are a frequent phenomenon. The inhabitants had developed anti-seismic practices, which at that time were still not adequate. The region had been struck by earthquakes in the past, and human experience of disaster was common in the coastal communities. // On 22 May 1960 an earthquake of magnitude 9.5 struck southern Chile, with its epicentre near Valdivia. The earthquake caused destruction in cities and communities, and it was followed by a tsunami that reached the shores of the Pacific. Losses of life were heavy, and many inhabitants lost their homes. The response of the authorities and residents to tsunami warnings was uneven. // The Valdivia earthquake is regarded as the strongest ever recorded with instruments, and its study helped science to understand better the structure of the tectonic plates. The disaster prompted Chile to develop better tsunami warning systems. The event remained as a critical lesson in earthquake safety. The tragedy contributed to international cooperation for the monitoring of tsunamis in the Pacific.

analysis|05-22|1990|Ενώνονται το Βόρειο και το Νότιο Υεμένη|North and South Yemen Unite|Yemen was divided for decades into two states, North Yemen and South Yemen, which had a colonial past with Britain and followed a socialist path. Relations between the two states were often strained, with border clashes. The idea of unification had always been present in the political discourse of the country. North Yemen had developed parliamentary elements, while South Yemen was governed by a party with socialist principles. // On 22 May 1990 the two states officially united and created the Republic of Yemen, with a joint government and parliament. The union came after negotiations and strengthened hopes for peace and development. The moment was linked with the end of the Cold War. The unification provided for a common constitutional organisation and the gradual completion of institutions, with consultations lasting months. // The union did not succeed in removing political differences. A few years later, in 1994, a civil war broke out in the south, which ended with the defeat of the separatists. Yemen continued to face economic and political problems, and the history of the union remains an example of the difficult synthesis of historical divisions. The unity of Yemen remains one of the basic issues of its political life, and the debate about federalisation continues.

analysis|05-23|1618|Η Αποβολή από το Παράθυρο της Πράγας|The Defenestration of Prague|The Letter of Majesty of 1609 had guaranteed freedoms, but its interpretation remained contested and a source of conflict. The Protestants of Bohemia felt that their rights, which had been secured in the past, were threatened by imperial decisions. Discontent had accumulated for years. // The act of 23 May 1618 was a symbolic and violent response by the nobles. The two officials were not killed, but the action opened the way to political and military rivalry between the Habsburgs and the Protestant powers of Germany. The confrontation peaked when the representatives of Bohemia gathered at the castle to protest against violations of the liberties that had been granted in the past. // This beginning led to the Thirty Years' War, which lasted until 1648 and left great devastation in central Europe. The Peace of Westphalia put an end to the war, and Prague remains in history as the place where the great conflict began. The conflict provided the spark for one of the most destructive periods of European history. This development is still discussed as an example of the relationship between political and religious freedom.

analysis|05-23|1934|Σκοτώνονται οι Μπόνι και Κλάιντ|Bonnie and Clyde Are Killed|The Great Depression had struck America with bank failures and mass unemployment, and public opinion was dissatisfied. Clyde Barrow and Bonnie Parker became known during the Great Depression, when unemployment and poverty led many Americans to view robbers with sympathy. The couple travelled through many states and committed robberies and murders. Their photographs spread widely and made them famous. // On 23 May 1934 police officers, led by a former officer of the Texas State Police, ambushed them near Louisiana and opened fire. The ambush was the result of a long investigation and cooperation between states. The state police had intensified their investigations, and the federal authorities cooperated to capture them. The news of their death spread immediately and aroused great interest. // Their death is regarded as the symbolic end of an era of robberies that fascinated the world. Their story has been the subject of books and films, and the image of the couple remains part of American popular culture. The case also showed how the police and the media shaped the public image of crime. The story of the two outlaws influenced American cinema, and the 1967 film renewed interest in that era.
